parole.significato: Fully sufficient; found in copious supply; in great quantity; overflowing.

parole.significato: Sloth, slothfulness, especially as inducing general listlessness and apathy.

parole.significato: A registry of pecuniary transactions; a written or printed statement of business dealings or debts and credits, and als…

parole.significato: A purveyor of provisions; a provedore.

parole.significato: A state of being acquainted with a person; originally indicating friendship, intimacy, but now suggesting a slight know…

parole.significato: A bookcase; a library or archive.

parole.significato: To charge (someone) with a crime; to impeach.

parole.significato: Of or relating to appeals; appellate.

parole.significato: A respondent.

parole.significato: Full of ardor; expressing passion, spirit, or enthusiasm.

parole.significato: Great warmth of feeling; fervor; passion.

parole.significato: A protective layer over a body, vehicle, or other object intended to deflect or diffuse damaging forces.

parole.significato: The crime of deliberately starting a fire with intent to cause damage.

parole.significato: An act of finding out or observing by spying or looking; an espial or espying.
parole.testo: From Middle English aspie, espie (“covert investigation or observation, scouting, spying; information obtained through spying; secret and treacherous plan, plot; treachery; a scout or spy”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman espie, Old French espie, from espier (verb): see further at etymology 1.

parole.significato: An attorney who sufficiently excuses the absence of another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman essoigniour, from Old French essoignier. By surface analysis, essoin + -er.

parole.significato: Previously owned; secondhand.
parole.testo: From Middle English estat, from Anglo-Norman estat and Old French estat (French: état), from Latin status. Doublet of state and status.

parole.significato: To impede or bar by estoppel.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English estoppen (“to prevent (conception)”), from Anglo-Norman and Old French estoper, from a Late Latin stuppō.

parole.significato: An animal that has escaped from its owner; a wandering animal whose owner is unknown. An animal cannot be an estray whe…
parole.testo: From Middle English astrai, from Anglo-Norman estray, from the Old French verb estraier. Etymological doublet with stray.

parole.significato: A kind of widemouthed pitcher or jug with a shape like a vase and a handle, and originally used for carrying water.
parole.testo: From Middle English ewer, from Anglo-Norman or Old French ewer, eawer (modern French évier), from Latin aquārium, from aqua (“water”). Doublet of aquarium.

parole.significato: The act of excepting or excluding; exclusion; restriction by taking out something which would otherwise be included, as…
parole.testo: From Middle English exception, excepcioun, from Anglo-Norman excepcioun, from Old French excepcion, from Latin exceptiō. Equivalent to except + -ion.

parole.significato: A spending or consuming, often a disbursement of funds.
parole.testo: From Middle English expense, from Anglo-Norman expense and Old French espense, from Late Latin expēnsa, from Latin expendō. See expend. Doublet of speso.

parole.significato: State or condition of not meeting a desirable or intended objective, opposite of success.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman failer, from Old French faillir (“to fail”). Equivalent to fail + -ure.

parole.significato: Culpability; the responsibility for a blameworthy event.
parole.testo: From Middle English faute, faulte, from Anglo-Norman faute, Old French faute, from Vulgar Latin *fallita (“shortcoming”), feminine of *fallitus, in place of Latin falsus, perfect passive participle of fallō (“deceive”). parole.significato: the performing of an act, especially out of one's duty.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman fesance, from Old French faisance (“action, deed, enactment”), from faisant, present participle of faire.

parole.significato: A relatively rare or difficult accomplishment.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Anglo-Norman fet (“action, deed”), from Old French fait, from Latin factum, from facere (“to do, to make”). Doublet of fact.

parole.significato: To ascribe the greatest importance to something within a certain context.
parole.testo: From Middle English feture, from Anglo-Norman feture, from Old French faiture, from Latin factūra, from Latin factus, from Latin faciō (“do, make”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put, place, set”). Doublet of facture.

parole.significato: A woman.
parole.testo: From Middle English feme, from Anglo-Norman feme (“woman”), from Old French femme, from Latin fēmina. Doublet of femina, femme, and hembra.

parole.significato: Fierce.
parole.testo: From Middle English fer, from Anglo-Norman fer, from Old French fier. Compare Latin ferus (“wild”).

parole.significato: The fruit of the fig tree, pear-shaped and containing many small seeds.
parole.testo: From Middle English fige, fygge (also fyke, from Old English fīc, see fike), borrowed from Anglo-Norman figue, borrowed from Old French figue, from Old Occitan figa, from Vulgar Latin *fīca (“fig”), from Latin fīcus (“fig tree”), from a pre-Indo European language, perhaps Phoenician 𐤐𐤂 (pg, literall

parole.significato: Son of; especially used for the illegitimate sons of royalty.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman fitz, from Old French fiz (modern fils), from Latin fīlius (“son”).

parole.significato: The visible part of fire; a stream of burning vapour or gas, emitting light and heat.
parole.testo: From Middle English flawme, blend of Old French flame and flambe, flamble, the first from Latin flamma, the second from Latin flammula, diminutive of flamma, both from pre-Latin *fladma; Proto-Italic *flagmā, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to shimmer, gleam, shine”). parole.significato: A soft cloth material originally woven from wool, today often combined with cotton or synthetic fibers.
parole.testo: From Middle English flaunneol, from Anglo-Norman flanelle (compare Norman flianné), diminutive of Old French flaine, floene (“coarse wool”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *wlānos, *wlanā (“wool”) (compare Welsh gwlân, Breton gloan), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wĺ̥h₁neh₂. More at wool.

parole.significato: Debris floating in a river or sea, in particular fragments from a shipwreck.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman floteson, from Old French flotaison (“a floating”), from floter (“to float”), of Germanic origin (See float.), + -aison, from Latin -atio.

parole.significato: To shape a metal by heating and hammering.
parole.testo: From Middle English forgen, from Anglo-Norman forger and Old French forgier, from Latin fabrico (“to frame, construct, build”). Doublet of fabricate.

parole.significato: The act of forging metal into shape.
parole.testo: Recorded since 1574; from forge + -ery, from Middle English forgen, via Anglo-Norman forger, from Old French forgier, from Latin fabricārī (“to frame, construct, fabricate”), itself from fabrica (“workshop; construction”), from faber (“workman, smith”). (fake): Compare typologically Russian кова́рны

parole.significato: A female founder (“one who founds or establishes”).
parole.testo: From Middle English founderess, founderesse, foundress (“female founder or builder of a city; female founder or benefactor of a religious house; (figuratively) female inventor or originator; (figuratively) a source”) [and other forms]; from founder, foundere, foundour (“founder or builder of a build

parole.significato: A freeholder, especially as belonging to a class of landowners in the 14th and 15th century ranking at the bottom of th…
parole.testo: From Middle English frankelein (“freeholder”), from Anglo-Norman fraunclein (“a landowner of free, but not noble birth”), from Old French fraunc (“free”), from Frankish *Frankō (“Frank”, literally “freeman”) + Old French -lein (“-ling”), from Frankish *-ling (“-ling”). More at frank, -ling.

parole.significato: To alarm or frighten (someone or something).

parole.significato: A person who sells, makes, repairs, alters, cleans, or otherwise deals in pelts or in clothing made of fur.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman, from Old French forreor, from fourrer (“to line or trim with fur”).

parole.significato: A saddle tree maker.
parole.testo: From Middle English fuster, fuystour, fuystor, from Anglo-Norman fuster, Old French fuyster, fust, ultimately from Latin fūstis. Compare French fût, Old French fustier.

parole.significato: Food waste material of any kind.
parole.testo: From late Middle English garbage (“the offal of a fowl, giblets, kitchen waste”, originally “refuse, what is purged away”), from Anglo-Norman, from Old French garber (“to refine, make neat or clean”), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *garwijan (“to make ready”). parole.significato: Something that garnishes; a decoration, adornment or embellishment
parole.testo: From Middle English garnetture, from Anglo-Norman garniture, gerneiture, from Old French garneture (“accessory for a saddle”), from Old French garnir, guarnir, from Frankish *warnijan (“to prevent, deny”).

parole.significato: In a cautious and delicate manner; (very) carefully or cautiously.
parole.testo: The second element is -ly; the first element may be Anglo-Norman gençur or Old French gençor, gensor, comparative forms (also attested as positives) of gent (“beautiful, noble, pleasant, courteous”). parole.significato: To exalt, or give glory or praise to (something or someone).
parole.testo: From Middle English glorifien, from Anglo-Norman and Old French glorifier, from Late Latin glōrificō, from Latin glōria + -ficō (“to make”). By surface analysis, glory + -fy. parole.significato: Exhibiting attributes, qualities, or acts that are worthy of or receive glory.
parole.testo: From Middle English glorious, from Anglo-Norman glorius and Old French glorïos, from Latin glōriōsus. Displaced native Middle English wulderful, from Old English wuldorfull (“glorious”), among other terms. Equivalent to glory + -ous.

parole.significato: To make and administer the public policy and affairs of; to exercise sovereign authority in.
parole.testo: From Middle English governen, governe, from Anglo-Norman and Old French governer, guverner, from Latin gubernō, from Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, drive, govern”). Displaced native Old English wealdan, whence modern dialectical English wald (“to govern”).

parole.significato: A killer whale (Orcinus orca).
parole.testo: From Middle English *grampas, grappays, grapas, graspeys, from Anglo-Norman grampais, Old French graspois, craspois (“whale, (salted) whale meat; blubber; seal”), from Medieval Latin craspicis (literally “fat fish”), from Latin crassus (“fat”) + piscis (“fish”).

parole.significato: Large, senior (high-ranking), intense, extreme, or exceptional
parole.testo: From Middle English grand, grond, graund, graunt, from Anglo-Norman graunt, from Old French grant, from Latin grandis. Doublet of grande and grandee.

parole.significato: A member of the Grange, National Grange of the Patrons of Husbandry, an association representing farmers.
parole.testo: From Middle English graunger, from Anglo-Norman granger, variant of Old French grangier, from grange, perhaps corresponding to Medieval Latin granicārium, from Vulgar Latin *granica, from Latin granum.

parole.significato: A grapnel (small anchor).
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman, from Old French grapil, grapin. Compare modern French grappin.

parole.significato: A small anchor, having more than two flukes, used for anchoring a small vessel.
parole.testo: From Middle English grapnel, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French grapil, grapin. Compare modern French grappin.

parole.significato: A stone or metal flat plate or surface on which food is fried or baked.
parole.testo: From Middle English gridil, from Anglo-Norman gredil, variant of Old French greil, from Latin crāticulum, diminutive of crātis. Doublet of grill (“grid of wire”), from the same Old French and Latin sources, doublet of grate.

parole.significato: Causing grief, pain, or sorrow.
parole.testo: From Middle English grevous, from Anglo-Norman grevous, from Old French grever, from Latin gravō (“to burden”). Developed in the 13th century. Equivalent to grief + -ous.

parole.significato: Astuteness often marked by a certain sense of cunning or artful deception.
parole.testo: From Middle English gile, from Anglo-Norman gile, from Old French guile (“deception”), from Frankish *wīl (“ruse”), from Proto-Germanic *wīlą, from Proto-Indo-European *wey- (“to turn, bend”). Cognate via Proto-Germanic with wile.

parole.significato: A prepared channel in a surface, especially at the side of a road adjacent to a curb, intended for the drainage of wate…
parole.testo: From Middle English gutter, guttur, goter, from Anglo-Norman guttere, from Old French goutiere (French gouttière), ultimately from Latin gutta (“drop”).

parole.significato: A saltwater fish, Melanogrammus aeglefinus, of the North Atlantic, important as a food fish.
parole.testo: From Middle English haddok. Compare Anglo-Norman hadoc from Old French hadot, probably from an English source. parole.significato: A large basket, usually with a cover, used for the packing and carrying of articles or small animals.
parole.testo: From Middle English hamper, contracted from hanaper, hanypere, from Anglo-Norman hanaper, Old French hanapier, hanepier (“case for holding a large goblet or cup”), from hanap (“goblet, drinking cup”), from Frankish *hnapp (“cup, bowl, basin”), from Proto-Germanic *hnappaz (“cup, bowl”). More at harry.

parole.significato: Demeanour, behaviour, comportment.
parole.testo: From Middle English havour, from Anglo-Norman aveyr, Old French aveir.

parole.significato: Totally reprehensible.
parole.testo: From Middle English heynous, from Anglo-Norman hainous, heinous (compare French haineux) from Old French haïr, hadir (“to hate”) (compare Old French en-hadir (“to become filled with hate”)), from Frankish *hattjan (“to hate”) (compare Middle English hetien). parole.significato: Extremely or shockingly ugly.
parole.testo: From Middle English hidous, from Anglo-Norman hidous, from Old French hideus, hydus (“that which inspires terror”), from earlier hisdos, from Old French hisda (“horror, fear”), of uncertain and disputed origin. parole.significato: A hoarding (temporary structure used during construction).
parole.testo: From Middle English hord, whorde, from Anglo-Norman hurde and Old French hourd, hourt (“barrier, palisade”), from Middle Dutch horde, from Old Dutch *hurd, from Proto-West Germanic *hurdi (“wickerwork, braiding of branches, hurdle, scaffolding, military company”).

parole.significato: A three-sided box mounted on a pole for carrying bricks, mortar, or other construction materials over the shoulder.
parole.testo: Probably an alteration of hot (“(Northern England, Scotland) large basket for carrying earth, etc.”), from Middle English hott, hote, hotte (“large basket or pannier for carrying earth, etc.; unit of measure for grain; hut or shed (perhaps originally of wattlework); lump of dirt (?)”) [and other for

parole.significato: To sacrifice (chiefly an animal) to be completely burned.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English holocaust (“burnt offering”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman holocauste, Old French holocauste, olocauste (modern French holocaust), from Late Latin holocaustum, from Ancient Greek ὁλόκαυστον (holókauston), the neuter form of ὁλόκαυστος (holókaustos, “who

parole.significato: Recognition of importance or value; respect; veneration (of someone, usually for being morally upright or successful).
parole.testo: From Middle English honour, honor, honur, from Anglo-Norman honour, honur, from Old French honor, from Latin honor. parole.testo: From Middle English ides, idus, from Anglo-Norman and Old French ides, from Latin īdūs, a fourth-declension plurale tantum, from the Latin practice of treating most recurring calendrical days as plurals. parole.significato: The result of being impaired.
parole.testo: From Middle English empeirement, empeyrement, emparement, from Anglo-Norman empairement, emperement, enpeirement, from Old French ampirement, anpirement, enperement, equivalent to impair + -ment.

parole.significato: Discussion, especially before some action is taken; conference, debate.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Anglo-Norman emparlance, from the verb Old French emparler.

parole.significato: To hinder, impede, or prevent.
parole.testo: From Middle English empechen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman empecher, from Old French empeechier (“to hinder”), from Latin impedicāre (“to fetter”). Cognate with French empêcher (“to prevent”).

parole.significato: To make poor.
parole.testo: From Middle English empoverishen, impoverishen, empoverischen, enpoverisshen, Anglo-Norman empoveriss-, from Old French empoverir, from em- + povre, from Latin pauper (“poor”) (English poor).

parole.significato: The action of impoverishing someone.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman empoverissement, from the Old French verb empoverir. By surface analysis, impoverish + -ment.

parole.significato: A confinement in a place, especially a prison or a jail, especially as punishment for a crime.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman emprisonement, from Old French emprisonnement. See imprison + -ment.

parole.significato: To make (something) better; to increase the value or productivity (of something).
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman emprouwer, from Old French en- + prou (“profit”), from Vulgar Latin prode (“advantageous, profitable”).

parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman endenture, from Old French endenteure, from endenter (“to dent”). The name of the contract derives from the irregular dent-shaped cut (indentation) used to prove the authenticity of the two parts, similar to a chirograph.

parole.significato: The passing of title to an estate upon death.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English enheritaunce, inheritaunce, borrowed from Anglo-Norman, Old French enheritaunce, from enheriter. By surface analysis, inherit + -ance.

parole.significato: One of a series of parts, whether equal or unequal to the other parts of the series, of a given entity or a given proce…
parole.testo: A 1732 alteration of estallment, from Anglo-Norman estaler (“fix payments”), from Old French estal (“fixed position”), from Old High German stal (“stall", "standing place”) The sense of "part of a whole produced in advance of the rest" is from 1823.

parole.significato: A decorative element found especially in early medieval art
parole.testo: From Middle English entrelacen, from Anglo-Norman entrelacer, from Old French inter- + lacer (“weave”).

parole.significato: To convert, convince, or win over with flattery or wiles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman enveugler, alteration of aveugler (“to blind, to delude”), from Old French avogle (“without eyes”), from Late Latin ab oculīs (“without eyes”, literally “away from the eyes”). parole.significato: A piece of armour for the leg (especially below the knee), a greave.
parole.testo: From Middle English iambeau(s) (compare jamber), from an Anglo-Norman [Term?] derivative of Old French jambe (“leg”): compare Old French jambiere. See jamb (noun). Compare lamboy(s).

parole.significato: A rattling metallic sound; a clang.
parole.testo: From Middle English jangle (“gossip, idle talk; a dispute”), from Anglo-Norman jangle and Old French jangle (“gossip, idle talk; a dispute”), from Old French jangler (“to chatter, gossip; to argue noisily; to bawl”): see further at etymology 1. parole.significato: Items that have been or are about to be ejected from a boat or balloon to lighten the vessel.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman getteson, from Old French getaison, from geter, jeter (modern French: would be *jetaison like pendaison); possibly from a Vulgar Latin *iectātiō, from *iectātus < iectāre, from Latin iactō. Doublet of jetsam.

parole.significato: A precious or semi-precious stone; gem, gemstone.
parole.testo: From Middle English juel, jewel, juwel, jeuel, jowel, from Anglo-Norman juel, from Old French jouel, joel, joïel, hence French joyau, of uncertain origin. parole.significato: A person whose job is making, repairing or selling jewelry.
parole.testo: From Middle English jueler, from Anglo-Norman jueler, or Old French juelier. By surface analysis, jewel + -er.

parole.significato: A diary or daily record of a person, organization, vessel etc.; daybook.
parole.testo: From Middle English journal, from Anglo-Norman jurnal (“daily”), from Old French jornel (“day”) (whence modern French journal), from Latin diurnālis, from diurnus (“of the day”). Doublet of diurnal and the journal from French.

parole.significato: To sit in judgment on; to pass sentence on (a person or matter).
parole.testo: From Middle English jugen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman juger, from Old French jugier, from Latin iūdicāre. Doublet of judicate. Partly displaced native deem.

parole.significato: A house or shelter for a dog.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱwṓ From Middle English kenel, kenell, borrowed from Anglo-Norman *kenil, northern variant of Old French chenil, from Vulgar Latin *canīle, from Latin canis.

parole.significato: Negligence in one's duty.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman laches, from Old French lachesse (“laxness”), from laschier, from Vulgar Latin laxico, frequentative of Latin laxo (“relax, moderate, weaken”).

parole.significato: A cool room in a domestic house where food is stored.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English larder, from Anglo-Norman larder and Old French lardier, from Latin lardārium. By surface analysis, lard + -er.

parole.significato: Synonym of interpreter.
parole.testo: From Middle English latyner, latynier (also latymer), from Anglo-Norman latimer, from Old French latinier, latimier, etc., from Latin latinārius, from lingua Latina + -ārius (“-ary”). Compare Old English Lǣdenware (“a Latin-speaker, Roman”). Doublet of latimer.

parole.significato: An evergreen shrub of species Laurus nobilis, having aromatic leaves of a lanceolate shape, with clusters of small, yel…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English laurer, laurel, from Anglo-Norman lorer, from Old French lorier, from Vulgar Latin *laurārius, from Latin laurus (“laurel”). Doublet of loureiro.

parole.significato: Loyal, honest.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English leel, lel, borrowed from Anglo-Norman leal and Old French leial, from Latin lēgālis. Doublet of loyal and legal.

parole.significato: loyalty, fealty
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman lealté, one of the variants of Old French loiauté.

parole.significato: To grant a lease as a landlord; to let.
parole.testo: From Middle English *lesen, from Anglo-Norman *leser, Old French lesser, laisier (“to let, let go”), partly from Latin laxō (“to loose”) and partly from Old High German lāzan (“to let, let go, release”) (German lassen), cognate with Old English lǣtan (“to allow, let go, leave, rent”) whence let.

parole.significato: Freedom provided by the cessation of activities.
parole.testo: From Middle English leyser, from Anglo-Norman leisir, variant of Old French loisir (“to enjoy oneself”) (Modern French loisir survives as a noun), substantive use of a verb, from Latin licēre (“be permitted”). Displaced native Old English ǣmetta.

parole.significato: To impose (a tax or fine) to collect monies due, or to confiscate property.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman leve, from Old French levee, from lever (“to raise”), from Latin lēvāre (“to raise, lift”).

parole.significato: lickerish; lecherous; eager; lustful.
parole.testo: From Middle English likerous, lykerous, likrus, from Anglo-Norman *likerous, *lekerous (“dainty”), apparently an unassibilated variant (compare lekeor, leckeur variants of lecheor, lichieor (“glutton, lecher”)) of Old French *lecherous ("dainty, wanton"; > English lecherous); see lecherous.

parole.significato: A free and independent person; specifically, a lord paramount; a sovereign.

parole.significato: The lowest junior commissioned officer rank(s) in many military forces, often Army and Marines.
parole.testo: From Middle English lieutenant, lieftenaunt, from Anglo-Norman lieutenant, lyutenaunt, leu tenant, leu tenaunt (“deputy, lieutenant”), from Old French lieu (“place”) + tenant (“holder”). Doublet of locum tenens and stadtholder.

parole.testo: From Middle English turbot, turbut, from Anglo-Norman turbut, Old French turbot, torbot, from Old Swedish tornbut, from törn (“thorn”) + but (“butt, flatfish”).

parole.significato: In a wine bottle, the empty space between the cork and the top of the wine.
parole.testo: From Middle English ulage, from Anglo-Norman ulliage, from *ullier (“to fill a partially empty cask”), from Old French oel (“bunghole”, literally “eye”), from Latin oculus (“eye”). See French ouillage.

parole.testo: From Middle English umbrell, umbrel, probably from Anglo-Norman umbrail, from Old French ombrail, ombral, from ombrel (“shade”), from ombre + -el, from Latin umbra; compare French ombrelle. By surface analysis, umb(e)r + -el.

parole.significato: Oneness: the state or fact of being one undivided entity.

parole.significato: Use, practise, exercise.
parole.testo: From Middle English ure, from Anglo-Norman *ure, Old French uevre (modern French œuvre), from Latin opera (“work, labor”). Doublet of oeuvre, opera, and opus.

parole.significato: Habit, practice.
parole.testo: From Middle English usage, from Anglo-Norman and Old French usage. By surface analysis, use + -age.

parole.significato: A person, in a church, cinema etc., who escorts people to their seats.
parole.testo: From Middle English ussher, uscher, usscher, from Anglo-Norman usser and Old French ussier, uissier (“porter, doorman”) (compare French huissier), from Vulgar Latin *ustiārius (“doorkeeper”), from Latin ōstiārius, from ōstium (“door”). parole.significato: A person who loans money to others and charges interest, particularly at an exorbitant, exploitative, or illegal rate.
parole.testo: Anglo-Norman, from Old French usurier, Latin ūsūra (“interest”).

parole.significato: An extended trip or journey away from home for rest or pleasure.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English vacation, vacacion, vacacioun, from Anglo-Norman vacacioun, from Old French vacacion, vacation, from Latin vacātiō. Equivalent to vacate + -ion.

parole.testo: From Middle English vagraunt, vagaraunt (“having no proper employment; having a tendency to go astray or wander; wayward”), from Anglo-Norman vagarant, wakerant, waucrant (“vagrant”) and Old French walcrant, waucrant (“roaming, wandering”); see further at etymology 1.

parole.significato: A short curtain that usually hangs along the top edge of a window.
parole.testo: From Middle English valance, valans, valaunce, valence, valons. Origin uncertain. Probably from Anglo-Norman valaunce, valence, from valer (“go down, let down”), aphetic form of Old French avaler (“to descend, go down”).

parole.significato: The quality of being valiant; heroism, bravery or valour.
parole.testo: From Middle English valiaunce, from Anglo-Norman vaillaunce and Old French vaillance.

parole.significato: An elongated depression cast between hills or mountains, often with a river flowing through it.
parole.testo: From Middle English valeye, valey, from Anglo-Norman valey, Old French valee (compare French vallée), from Latin vallēs/vallis. Doublet of vlei and vly. Displaced native dene, from dene and partially displaced native dale, from dæl.

parole.significato: Individually sustained verve or passion.
parole.testo: From Middle English valour, from Anglo-Norman valour, from Latin valor. Doublet of valure.

parole.significato: To speak boastfully.
parole.testo: From Middle English vaunten, from Anglo-Norman vaunter, variant of Old French vanter, from Latin vānus (“vain, boastful”).

parole.significato: The vanguard.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English vawarde, late form of vantwarde, aphetism of Anglo-Norman avantwarde, a variant of Old French avant-guarde. Doublet of avant-garde and vanguard.

parole.significato: Revenge taken for an insult, injury, or other wrong.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman vengeaunce, from Old French vengeance, venjance, from vengier (“to avenge”). Analysable as venge + -ance.

parole.significato: A room in a church where the clergy put on their vestments and where these are stored; also used for meetings and class…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman vesterie, from Old French vestiaire (“room for vestments, dressing room”), from Latin vestiarium (“wardrobe”). Doublet of vestiary.

parole.significato: A covering of, or like, clothing.
parole.testo: From Middle English vesture (noun) and vesturen (verb), from Anglo-Norman, from Old French vesteüre, from Vulgar Latin vestītūra (“clothing”), from Latin vestītus, perfect passive participle of vestiō (“to clothe”), from vestis (“garment”).

parole.significato: An item of food.
parole.testo: From Middle English vyaund, from Anglo-Norman and Old French viande, from Late Latin *vivanda, from Latin vīvenda, from the verb vīvō (“to live”). Compare victual, viando. parole.significato: Visual perception.
parole.testo: From Middle English vewe, from Anglo-Norman vewe, from Old French veue f (French vue f), feminine past participle of veoir (“to see”) (French voir). Cognate with Italian vedere, as well as Portuguese and Spanish ver. Doublet of veduta and vista.

parole.significato: Physically strong and active.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman vigrus, from Old French vigoros (French vigoureux), from Medieval Latin vigorosus, from Latin vigor. Doublet of vigoroso.

parole.significato: Morally low; base; despicable.
parole.testo: From Middle English vile, vyle, vyl, from Anglo-Norman ville, Old French vil, vile, from Latin vīlis.

parole.significato: The smallest administrative unit of land in feudal England, corresponding to the Anglo-Saxon tithing and the modern par…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman vill, from Old French vile (“farm, country estate”) (French ville (“town”)), from Latin vīlla. Doublet of villa and ville.

parole.significato: Evil or wicked character or behaviour.
parole.testo: From Middle English vileinie, vileynye, from Anglo-Norman vilenie, from Old French vilanie.

parole.significato: The yield of grapes or wine from a vineyard or district during one season.
parole.testo: From Middle English vendage, vyndage, from Anglo-Norman vendenge, from Old French vendage, vendenge (cognate with French vendange), from Latin vindēmia (“a gathering of grapes, vintage”), from vīnum (“wine”) + dēmō (“take off or away, remove”), from de (“of; from, away from”) + emō (“take”).

parole.significato: An instrument consisting of two jaws, closing by a screw, lever, cam, or the like, for holding work, as in filing.
parole.testo: From Middle English vis, vys, vice (“screw”), from Anglo-Norman vyz, vice, from Old French vis (“screw”), from Latin vītis f (“vine”). Probably akin to English withe.

parole.significato: The sense or ability of sight.
parole.testo: From Middle English visioun, from Anglo-Norman visioun, from Old French vision, from Latin vīsiō (“vision, seeing”), noun of action from the perfect passive participle visus (“that which is seen”), from the verb videō (“to see”) + action noun suffix -iō.

parole.significato: The act of visiting, or an instance of being visited.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman visitacioun, from Old French visitacion, from Latin vīsitātiō. By surface analysis, visit + -ation.

parole.significato: Someone who visits someone else; someone staying as a guest.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle English visiter, visitere, equivalent to visit + -er; and partly from Middle English visitour, from Anglo-Norman visitour, from Old French visetëor. By surface analysis, visit + -or.

parole.testo: From Middle English viser, from Anglo-Norman viser and Old French visiere.

parole.significato: The preliminary phase of a jury trial in which the jurors are examined and selected.
parole.testo: Anglo-Norman for “to say the truth”, from Old French voir (“true, truth”) + dire (“to say”), from Latin vērum + dīcere.

parole.testo: Borrowed into Middle English from Anglo-Norman vultur, from Old French voutoir, voutre, from Latin vultur, voltur. Displaced native Old English ūf.

parole.significato: To relinquish (a right etc.); to give up claim to; to forgo.
parole.testo: From Middle English weyven (“to avoid, renounce”), from Anglo-Norman weyver (“to abandon, allow to become a waif”), from Old French waif (“waif”), from gaiver (“to abandon”), ultimately of Scandinavian/North Germanic origin; see weyver.

parole.significato: A guard or watchman.
parole.testo: From Middle English wardein, from Anglo-Norman wardein, from warder (“to guard”), variant of Old French guarder (“to guard”) (whence modern French garder, also English guard), from Proto-Germanic *wardāną; related to Old High German wartēn (“to watch”). parole.significato: To cure or heal (an illness or a person).
parole.testo: From Middle English warysshen, from Anglo-Norman waris-, the present participle stem of warir, from Old French guarir (modern guérir), from Frankish *warjan, from Proto-Germanic *warjaną. Compare guarish.

parole.significato: A person who is actively engaged in battle, conflict or warfare; a soldier or combatant.
parole.testo: From Middle English werreour, from Anglo-Norman werreur, Old French guerroiier (“fighter, combattant”), from Medieval Latin werra, from Frankish *werʀu (“confusion; quarrel”), from Proto-Indo-European *wers- (“to mix up, confuse, beat, thresh”).
